title: Recycling Update: How’s It Going?
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry on production) update their earlier episode on recycling, asking whether what people put in the bin actually gets recycled. They cover the recycling hierarchy (reduce, reuse, recycle), single-stream recycling and rising participation, aspirational recycling and contamination, the history of recycling from the Industrial Revolution through Earth Day and the nineties, US diversion rates and recycling rankings, how materials are sorted and reprocessed (paper, glass, steel, plastic with resin codes), China's 2017-2018 refusal of foreign recyclables and the resulting market disruption, criticisms of recycling, and a list of items people wrongly recycle (Starbucks cups, pizza boxes, plastic bags, styrofoam, diapers, bottle caps). The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Philip Zimbardo and the Stanford prison experiment.

segments.title: Opening and reasons for the recycling update
segments.summary: The hosts explain they are revisiting an early episode on recycling because recycling has changed, and they were not very good at it back then. They joke about the earlier Great Pacific Garbage Patch coverage and tease the China changes.

segments.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle hierarchy and single-stream recycling
segments.summary: They explain that recycling is the last of the three Rs, and that single-stream recycling has increased participation while also encouraging people to recycle items that cannot be recycled.

segments.title: Closing the loop, landfills and upcycling
segments.summary: They discuss the ideal of closing the materials loop, the role of landfills, how recycled materials degrade (downstream recycling), and upcycling examples such as turning a hubcap into a bird bath.

segments.title: History of recycling and US diversion rates
segments.summary: They trace recycling from the Industrial Revolution and pre-modern reuse through the post-war consumer boom, the post-Earth Day green movement, and the nineties heyday. They cite diversion statistics, with a peak around 2011, and note that waste generation has grown.

segments.title: Most recycled materials and international rankings
segments.summary: They go through the most recycled items in the US, with aluminum cans and corrugated boxes near the top and batteries, specifically lead acid batteries, at number one. They also compare the US with other countries and cities on recycling rankings.

segments.title: China's refusal of recyclables and the market collapse
segments.summary: They explain that China had been the largest buyer of foreign recyclables and then stopped accepting most of them in 2017-2018 because of contamination. Recyclables were diverted to landfills, and countries like Malaysia, India and Indonesia began buying more.

segments.title: Sorting and reprocessing paper, glass, steel and plastic
segments.summary: They describe how paper is pulped, deinked and reformed, how glass is sorted by color and reused or melted, how steel is recycled and shredded from cars, and how plastic is separated by density and classified by resin codes one through seven, including why bottle caps should stay attached.

segments.title: Criticisms of recycling and what not to recycle
segments.summary: They address criticisms such as false sense of security, the landfill-space argument, and the economic benefits of recycling. They list items that should not go in the bin, including Starbucks cups, greasy pizza boxes, plastic bags, styrofoam, dirty containers, and diapers.

segments.title: Listener mail: Zimbardo follow-up
segments.summary: A listener named Alex writes that he discovered Philip Zimbardo hosted the PBS series Discovering Psychology, which he watched in high school, and comments on the Stanford prison experiment.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and direct listeners to the website and email for more information.
